item.title: Your PC's second M.2 slot can do more than you think, and it costs almost nothing
item.itunes:title: Your PC's second M.2 slot can do more than you think, and it costs almost nothing
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When building a PC, it's easy to leave a second or sometimes even third M.2 NVMe slot sitting completely empty. You can actually use this spare slot to upgrade and give yourself some modern features like faster local networking (Wi-Fi 7/6e) or even extra utility ports.

M.2 slots aren't just narrow storage trays; they are direct physical breakouts of high-speed PCIe lanes and USB pathways coming straight off of your CPU and chipset. The vacant secondary M.2 slot on your motherboard is a hidden expansion goldmine.

By utilizing inexpensive specialized M.2 conversion and interface cards, you can actually transform a dormant slot on your motherboard into a multi-gigabit Ethernet port, wireless upgrade, or extra connectivity hub for essentially pocket change.

Your old PC doesn't need a new motherboard, just a $15 adapter and a faster drive

You don't need constant hardware upgrades.

4
By  Jasmine Mannan

M.2 slots are capable of so much more

You don't have to be limited to storage

Understanding what an M.2 slot actually is may help you find out how this is possible. The underlying bus architecture makes these M.2 slots so versatile. They're not just storage slots; they're actually PCIe lanes in disguise.

NVMe SSDs don't use a magical proprietary bus; they communicate directly over standard PCIe lanes, typically PCIe 3.0, 4.0, or 5.0 x4, and these are mapped straight to the motherboard. This means there are a range of different things that you can put into your spare M.2 slot: alternative expansion cards and adapters that give you access to a range of non-storage utilities.

Let's say your motherboard came with a legacy 1 GbE network port, but your home NAS and local network have moved to multi-gigabit speeds. You can actually upgrade to a multi-gigabit Ethernet port, like 2.5 GbE or even 10 GbE, with a spare M.2 slot by using a compact M.2 to Ethernet network interface card. This injects blazing-fast local speed transfers directly into the system without burning a precious full-size PCIe slot meant for a GPU.

You can also pick up modern Wi-Fi and Bluetooth modules. If you buy a non-Wi-Fi motherboard variant to save a couple of dollars at checkout, a spare M.2 A+E key slot or an adapter card lets you drop in an Intel AX210 module to instantly provision Wi-Fi 6E as well as Bluetooth 5.3.

And of course you can get expanded connectivity as well as specialized adapters, repurposing idle slots into alternative headers (such as adding specialized USB-C controllers or internal USB-E headers for front panel chassis integration when the motherboard lacks native connections).

Don't stuff your PC case

You might cause issues with your airflow

Unfortunately, something to keep in mind is that there are some real-world physical and electrical constraints behind upgrading a spare M.2 slot. Make sure that your motherboard is completely compatible before getting started.

The first thing to look out for is lane sharing and bandwidth conflicts. This is because, on some consumer chipsets, populating secondary M.2 slots can disable certain SATA ports or share bandwidth with PCIe expansion slots. You can check your motherboard's manual's block diagram for more information about whether or not this is the case for your specific model. If you're not using your SATA ports, then of course it's a no-brainer to go ahead with an M.2 expansion. But if you are, then it might not be worth disabling a load of your other SSDs just so you can get faster network speeds.

Another big issue can actually be the physical limitations, thanks to clearance constraints. Installing adapter cards or non-standard modules in a cramped mid-tower or small form factor case can require measuring clearances very carefully beneath large graphics cards or CPU air coolers. Poor placement can obstruct airflow or leave a high-power adapter with inadequate cooling, potentially raising component temperatures or causing thermal throttling.

How to make use of your secondary M.2 slot

Identify your key type

If you're considering making use of your secondary M.2 slots, here's how to get started. The first thing you want to do is actually audit your motherboard. You can have a look at it physically within your PC case to see if you see a secondary M.2 slot. If you do, then it might be time to look up your motherboard's digital manual and look specifically at the lane sharing matrix for your secondary M.2 slots (so you know whether or not it's worth investing in upgrades to implement).

Next, identify your key type. Determining whether your spare slot is an M key (for storage and PCIe x4) or an A/E key for wireless features will allow you to buy the correct adapter or module. For example, if you want to install Wi-Fi and Bluetooth capabilities but you only have an M key, then you need to ensure that you have the correct adapters in place; by simply installing the module itself, it will not work.

Lastly, secure and test. Install the hardware module that you have and make sure you're securing it with proper standoffs. This will prevent any damage happening to your components inside your case, especially if you ever move it around. Make sure that you're verifying the driver recognition in Device Manager or Linux kernel logs. If there's an issue with the device recognition in your Device Manager, then consult the module's handbook, but this might be down to the fact that it's purely not compatible with the slot you've installed it in.

Don't let your M.2 slot go to waste

You can add so many modern features to your PC

Stop letting motherboard real estate sit idle. PC builders often suffer from a narrow mindset when looking at motherboard layouts. If a slot isn't holding a graphics card or a primary boot drive, we write it off as useless, but a lot of modern buses are remarkably flexible. If you've got unused M.2 slots, then you might be leaving high-speed lanes sitting completely idle. For the price of a takeout lunch you can upgrade your PC's capabilities and squeeze every drop of value out of your hardware.

item.title: I ditched Lightroom for this snappy free alternative, and editing RAW on my phone has never been easier
item.itunes:title: I ditched Lightroom for this snappy free alternative, and editing RAW on my phone has never been easier
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Working with RAW on mobile isn't really something you think about until you actually have to do it, and then you realize every app for it is either paywalled or entirely paid. Lightroom Mobile is the default answer for most people, and sure it's free to download and use, but if you want to handle your RAW shots, Adobe puts up a paywall.

I lost my old DSLR in a move a while ago and have been relying on my phone since. There are tons of third-party apps that let you shoot in RAW on mobile, and I'm pretty settled on my existing stack, but to get decent RAW editing, you usually have to transfer the shots to a PC and use dedicated RAW software. Well, it turns out there's a mobile app that can handle them just as well on your phone, for free, called Snapseed.

RapidRAW is the free, open-source Lightroom alternative I've been waiting for

Editing photos is about to get a whole lot easier

8
By  João Carrasqueira

Lightroom for mobile is free, until you want to edit RAW

Everything you'd need for RAW work sits behind a subscription

Lightroom Mobile is one of those apps that's technically free and functionally not. You can sign in and edit JPEGS with basic sliders without paying, at least, that's the version Adobe wants you to try, and it's not bad actually. But the version you need if you want more advanced functions is Premium at around $5 a month (Adobe has started increasing this in some regions), or the Photography Plan.

Lightroom does actually have its own in-app camera that shoots DNG, and Adobe lets you edit those files for free, which sounds like a workaround until you actually try it. All you can really do without paying is nudge the basic sliders. Anything that makes shooting RAW worthwhile in the first place is paywalled, including the healing brush, geometry corrections, batch editing, presets, and more.

So you can technically edit RAW for free in Lightroom mobile, but you're limited in terms of how much. For some, this will be enough, but for anyone who actually wants to transform their RAW shots, it's worth looking elsewhere.

5 best Lightroom alternative for open-source photo editing

Edit and organize your photos with secure privacy

By  Ruby Helyer

What Snapseed does with your RAW files

A ten-year-old app in a brand-new coat, and it costs nothing

Snapseed was built by Nik Software, bought by Google in 2012, and then more or less abandoned until we got version 3.0 in June 2025 and 4.0 in May 2026. That's more updates in one year than the app got in the entire decade before that.

The RAW format support is genuinely broad: DNG (which is what I shoot), Sony ARW, Canon CR2 and CR3, Nikon NEF, Fujifilm RAF, and Hasselblad FFF. All of them open directly with no conversion required or import catalog or cloud sync. When Snapseed detects a RAW file it launches a dedicated Develop tool first, which is where it really starts to get to work: exposure across four stops, temperature from 1,700K to over 8,000K, tint, structure, shadow control, contrast, saturation, all working on the uncompressed sensor data before you even tweak anything else.

Then there's everything else. Snapseed has full RGB curves, selective adjustments with control-point precision, a proper healing tool, tune image, and details for sharpening. All of it's also non-destructive now. Every edit lives as a step in the Edit Stack, which you can reorder, tweak, or roll back weeks later. Lightroom's free tier has nothing to match this.

I quite like the object brush. You tap or trace a subject and on-device AI segmentation builds a mask hugging its edges. Then you apply exposure, curves, whatever, to just that subject. It's the free version of the AI Masking Lightroom locks behind Premium, and it actually works well on RAW files where you've got a little more headroom to push a masked exposure.

And to really put the cherry on top, there's no account or sign-in required, no ads, and zero paywalls. This app is genuinely completely free.

This open-source tool combines Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and After Effects - And it replaced all three for me

I didn't expect it to replace my entire Adobe setup

13
By  Nolen Jonker

My mobile RAW workflow

How I shoot and edit on a base-model iPhone

My iPhone 16 is the base model, so no ProRAW natively (that's still a Pro-only feature). So if I want true RAW, I need to go the third-party route. Halide is a pro-grade RAW shooter for iOS and I tried it out for a minute a while back, but unfortunately it is paid. So my pick now is Simple RAW Cam. It's free with some ads, and it captures uncompressed DNG straight to my camera roll with no export step.

From there it's just a matter of importing straight to Snapseed from my roll, and it opens into the Develop tool. Full RAW headroom for exposure and white balance recovery and no waiting on a cloud sync. Edits save to a Snapseed folder in my gallery non-destructively, the original DNG stays untouched, and export gives me a JPEG to share or a full-quality copy to keep. So the entire RAW loop lives on my phone.

I will say, Snapseed's file handling isn't Lightroom's catalog. If you're managing thousands of shoots across devices, Lightroom still wins on that front. For everything else, though, this is faster and cheaper.

8 open-source photo management tools for great library organization

Self-hosted and secure management tools to organize your photos

By  Ruby Helyer

A mobile RAW workflow that makes subscriptions feel silly

Snapseed isn't going to out-organize Lightroom on catalog-heavy work any time soon. But it does turn a mobile RAW workflow into something that actually feels doable when mobile RAW used to feel like a compromise. Tools like Snapseed have clearly caught up and the files also hold up under real editing.

item.title: After banning all Linux and Steam Deck players, Ubisoft's For Honor is free to keep until September 28th
item.itunes:title: After banning all Linux and Steam Deck players, Ubisoft's For Honor is free to keep until September 28th
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Ubisoft added competitive modes but banned Linux/SteamOS players over open-source kernel anti-cheat issues.
  • Free to keep on the Ubisoft Store until September 28; Steam and Epic list the Standard edition at ~90% off.
  • Linux/SteamOS users can't play online; kernel-level anti-cheat blocks access even if you bought it.

A little while ago, Ubisoft announced that it was introducing new competitive modes to its online multiplayer game, For Honor. In the same breath, it then announced that it was flat-out banning everyone playing on a Linux OS from playing, because it couldn't properly code a kernel-level anti-cheat when the kernel is open-source.

The Linux gaming community was pretty upset, especially those who had paid for the game, played past Steam's refund window, then got locked out of it (although one person got a refund after four tries). Now, to make matters worse, Ubisoft has made For Honor free to keep forever if you grab it before September 28th.

For Honor is free to keep on the Ubisoft Store

It's also at an extreme discount on other stores

Credit: Ubisoft

As spotted by Notebook Check, Ubisoft is currently holding a big sale on For Honor. You can grab it for free between now and September 28th if you pop over to the Ubisoft Store and grab it from there. If you'd rather purchase it from a different storefront, you can also grab it from Steam and the Epic Games Store. It's not free on either of those platforms, but they are both at a 90% discount, which does cut the cost down considerably.

It's worth noting that the free/90% off version doesn't give you all the bells and whistles; it is just the Standard version, after all. However, at least on Steam, the Gold and Ultimate editions are 85% off, so if you've had your eyes on either of those, now's a good time.

Just remember: if you use a Linux OS (and that includes SteamOS, which is based on a Linux distro called Arch), the anti-cheat won't let you play online, so don't get your hopes up for that.

Ubisoft bans Linux and Steam Deck users from For Honor because it "cannot meaningfully deploy protection"

There's not much you can do if you're affected.

52
By  Simon Batt

item.title: The Lenovo Yoga 9i was my favorite laptop from last year, and the new iteration is just as good
item.itunes:title: The Lenovo Yoga 9i was my favorite laptop from last year, and the new iteration is just as good
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I got hands-on with last year's Lenovo Yoga 9i, it was nothing short of a pleasure to use. Great keyboard, gorgeous screen, and an improved battery made it one of my favorite laptops of the year, and so when I got the opportunity to take their latest Yoga 9i for a spin, I'd be lying if I said I wasn't a bit excited.

This laptop checks a lot of the same boxes as its predecessor: you get a very well-built laptop with a slick design, and while it's definitely not going to win any value awards, it executes incredibly well on all the things that matter to someone who wants a great convertible laptop.

About this review: Lenovo provided a loan unit of the Lenovo Yoga 9i 2-in-1 Aura Edition (2026) for the purposes of this review. The company did not have any input into this article, nor did it see its contents before publishing.

Lenovo Yoga Slim 7i Aura Edition review: A good laptop

The Lenovo Yoga Slim 7i Aura Edition gets the job done at a reasonable price.

By  Rich Woods

Pricing and availability of the Lenovo Yoga 9i Aura Edition

The Lenovo Yoga 9i 2-in-1 Aura Edition is available on Lenovo's website starting at $2,380. At the time of writing, it can also be found at Best Buy for $2350 for the base spec, which is an Intel Core UItra 7 355 with 32 GB of LPDDR5X-7467, and a 1TB PCIe Gen 4 QLC SSD, upgradable to 2TB through the online configurator. At this time, that looks like the only spec available. The display is standard across both models, being the 12" 2.8K OLED.

A familiar design

The Yoga 9i is easy on the eyes in more ways than one

Lenovo stuck to their guns on the design of the Yoga 9i, and that's a good thing. I really enjoy the design from top to bottom, but there's some notable changes from last year's 9i.

First, the keyboard is almost identical, but they removed the rightmost column of keys that used to occupy the space under the Delete key. This bought them some more space on either side of the keyboard, but it also came at the cost of a fingerprint reader. Windows Hello via the IR Camera is good enough, but I would've liked the option on a laptop of this price.

Moving to the I/O, Lenovo has replaced one of the USB-C 20Gbps ports with a full-size HDMI 2.1 port, which is a welcome change. Some may have appreciated that extra non-Thunderbolt USB-C port, but to me, this is a worthwhile swap. You can also snap the new Yoga Pen Gen 2 to the back of the display with its neat little cover. When you close the laptop fully into tablet mode, that pen case does give a slight angle to the display, which does feel a bit better to use than if it were totally flat. Besides those changes, everything else is pretty much the same as far as the body of the laptop goes, which, again, is a good thing.

Moving on to the features that are relatively unchanged: the speakers on this laptop are still really solid. The forward-facing soundbar across the bottom hinge can fill a decently sized room at its highest volume. There are two woofers and two tweeters that have the Dolby Atmos seal of approval, and overall, this is one of the best-sounding laptops I've used for sure.

The display is that same 2.8K OLED from the previous year, and it looks just as good as it did. Lenovo removed the ability to kit this machine out with a full-fat 4K display, but for a screen of this size, the bump in sharpness wouldn't be worth the consequences for the battery, which is actually a bit smaller this year, coming in at 70Wh instead of 75Wh. Presumably, one of the keys behind that change is Panther Lake, which has a great showing in this chassis.

At full brightness or anywhere near it, you'll be reaching for the charger by the day's end or at the start of your next one, but with VRR on and even just a little bit of brightness management, this is easily an all-day machine.

item.title: These open-source Android apps are so good I ditched their mainstream rivals
item.itunes:title: These open-source Android apps are so good I ditched their mainstream rivals
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Between tech companies hiking prices, stuffing more features behind subscriptions, and seemingly finding a new way to squeeze money out of users every other week, it’s easy to feel a little cynical about the state of software right now.

One thing that consistently restores some of my faith in the internet, though, is the open-source community. There are developers out there building genuinely excellent apps, maintaining them for years, and giving them away for free without turning every useful feature into another monthly subscription.

Android is full of apps like this, and after spending some time digging through what’s out there, I’ve found a handful that are so good I’ve actually stopped using their more mainstream alternatives.

Breezy Weather

I just wanted to know if it was going to rain

I’ve never really understood why checking whether it’s going to rain needs to involve ads, subscriptions, news stories, and a dozen other things I never asked for. Breezy Weather strips all of that away. It’s completely free and open source, has no ads or trackers, and somehow still manages to be one of the most feature-packed weather apps I’ve used.

The biggest reason I prefer it over apps like AccuWeather and even the weather apps built into Android phones is that Breezy lets me choose where my weather data actually comes from. It supports more than 50 weather sources, including Open-Meteo, AccuWeather, OpenWeather, and several national weather services.

You can even use different providers for forecasts, current conditions, air quality, pollen, precipitation, and weather alerts, which is particularly useful if one source happens to be more accurate where you live.

Breezy can show hourly and daily forecasts, precipitation, wind, humidity, UV levels, air quality, pollen, visibility, atmospheric pressure, and even sun and moon information. Better yet, you can rearrange or hide the blocks you don’t care about, so having all of that data doesn’t mean scrolling through a cluttered mess every time you open the app.

There are still a couple of compromises. Breezy Weather isn’t available on the Play Store, so you’ll need to install it through GitHub, F-Droid, or another supported source, and it doesn’t have a weather radar. But considering there’s no premium tier hiding the good features, no ads getting in the way, and no unnecessary news feed desperately trying to keep me inside a weather app, those are compromises I’m more than willing to make.

OSS Document Scanner

It’s a scanner. Why was I paying for this?

As the name of the app suggests, it’s an open-source document scanner that lets you scan receipts, notes, forms, and multi-page documents, then export them as PDFs or images.

OSS Document Scanner can automatically detect the edges of a page, crop and straighten scans, enhance them with different filters, and even use OCR to make the text inside a scanned PDF searchable. The OCR models can be downloaded for offline use too, so the entire process can stay on your device.

There’s also a ridiculous amount of control hidden in the app’s settings. You can adjust PDF quality and compression, change how sensitive automatic document detection is, tweak auto-capture behavior, create custom file-name templates, lock the app behind biometrics, and even choose where scans are stored. It also supports bulk scanning and lets you merge, reorder, and edit pages before exporting them.

That last part is what really made Adobe feel a little excessive for what I actually need a scanner for. Adobe has plenty of advantages if you’re heavily invested in Acrobat or need its cloud and AI features, but I mostly just want to point my phone at a piece of paper and end up with a clean PDF. OSS Document Scanner does exactly that without requiring me to turn such a basic task into another subscription or cloud service.

Bitwarden

My passwords don’t need another monthly bill

Password managers are one of those apps I’m more than happy to pay for if I need to, but Bitwarden makes a pretty convincing argument that I shouldn’t have to. Its free plan lets you store unlimited passwords and use them across unlimited devices, while also giving you autofill, a password generator, passkey management, encrypted exports, and the ability to share vault items with one other person without paying anything.

That alone makes it a surprisingly capable alternative to something like 1Password or LastPass, but the fact that Bitwarden is open source is what really sets it apart for me. Its client and server code is publicly available for anyone to inspect, and if you don’t want to rely on Bitwarden’s own cloud infrastructure, you can even self-host the server yourself and keep your vault infrastructure under your own control. Your vault is protected using end-to-end, zero-knowledge encryption, so Bitwarden itself shouldn’t be able to see what you’ve stored inside it.

The Android app covers pretty much everything I actually want from a password manager too. It can save and autofill passwords in apps and websites, store cards, identities, and secure notes, generate credentials, and even save and autofill passkeys on supported versions of Android.

Open source doesn’t necessarily mean completely free, though, and Bitwarden does have a Premium tier. Features like the integrated TOTP authenticator, encrypted file attachments, emergency access, and more detailed vault-health reports require a subscription. Even so, the actual password-management part of the app is remarkably unrestricted on the free plan, and that’s ultimately the part I’d otherwise be paying another service for.

Organic Maps

Getting from A to B doesn’t require Google

Google Maps is one of those apps I’d always assumed would be nearly impossible to replace, but Organic Maps gets surprisingly close. It’s a completely free and open-source navigation app built on OpenStreetMap data, with detailed maps you can download and use entirely offline. There are no ads, trackers, mandatory accounts, or data collection either.

The fact that it works offline doesn’t mean you’re limited to simply looking at a map. Organic Maps supports turn-by-turn navigation with voice guidance for driving, walking, and cycling, along with public transport routes, offline search, hiking trails, cycling paths, contour lines, and elevation profiles. You can also import and export bookmarks and tracks using formats like GPX, KML, KMZ, and GeoJSON.

Organic Maps obviously can’t completely replicate everything Google Maps does. If I’m looking for live traffic information, detailed business reviews, or trying to figure out which restaurant nearby is actually worth going to, I’m

probably still opening Google Maps. But for simply getting somewhere, particularly somewhere I might not have reliable internet access, Organic Maps has made me realize just how much of Google Maps I don’t actually need.

LocalSend

The file-sharing app ecosystems should’ve given us

I like LocalSend enough that I’ve already written an entire article about it, and I still can’t recommend it enough. It’s essentially the cross-platform file-sharing tool I’ve always wanted AirDrop and Quick Share to be. Instead of locking you into one ecosystem, LocalSend works across Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, and Linux, so I can send a file from practically any device I own to any other one.

Using it is almost suspiciously simple. As long as both devices are connected to the same local network and have LocalSend open, they automatically discover each other. You choose a file, tap the device you want to send it to, accept the transfer on the other end, and you’re done. In my own testing, I actually found the whole process more seamless and at times faster than AirDrop, particularly because I wasn’t waiting around for the device I wanted to send something to finally appear.

The part I appreciate most, though, is that there’s no cloud involved. LocalSend discovers devices over your local network and transfers files directly between them rather than uploading them to some external server first. Its protocol uses HTTPS for encrypted transfers, and you don’t need an account or even an internet connection for it to work.

That also means I no longer need to send files to myself through Slack, WhatsApp, Google Drive, or some other service just because the two devices in front of me happen to run different operating systems. LocalSend does one incredibly simple thing, does it exceptionally well, and doesn’t care whose logo is on the devices I’m using.

The above are just a few of the open-source apps I absolutely can’t get enough of, and they’ve made it surprisingly easy to ditch some of the mainstream alternatives I’d been using for years.

Breezy Weather

I just wanted to know if it was going to rain

I’ve never really understood why checking whether it’s going to rain needs to involve ads, subscriptions, news stories, and a dozen other things I never asked for. Breezy Weather strips all of that away. It’s completely free and open source, has no ads or trackers, and somehow still manages to be one of the most feature-packed weather apps I’ve used.

The biggest reason I prefer it over apps like AccuWeather and even the weather apps built into Android phones is that Breezy lets me choose where my weather data actually comes from. It supports more than 50 weather sources, including Open-Meteo, AccuWeather, OpenWeather, and several national weather services.

You can even use different providers for forecasts, current conditions, air quality, pollen, precipitation, and weather alerts, which is particularly useful if one source happens to be more accurate where you live.

Breezy can show hourly and daily forecasts, precipitation, wind, humidity, UV levels, air quality, pollen, visibility, atmospheric pressure, and even sun and moon information. Better yet, you can rearrange or hide the blocks you don’t care about, so having all of that data doesn’t mean scrolling through a cluttered mess every time you open the app.

There are still a couple of compromises. Breezy Weather isn’t available on the Play Store, so you’ll need to install it through GitHub, F-Droid, or another supported source, and it doesn’t have a weather radar. But considering there’s no premium tier hiding the good features, no ads getting in the way, and no unnecessary news feed desperately trying to keep me inside a weather app, those are compromises I’m more than willing to make.

OSS Document Scanner

It’s a scanner. Why was I paying for this?

As the name of the app suggests, it’s an open-source document scanner that lets you scan receipts, notes, forms, and multi-page documents, then export them as PDFs or images.

OSS Document Scanner can automatically detect the edges of a page, crop and straighten scans, enhance them with different filters, and even use OCR to make the text inside a scanned PDF searchable. The OCR models can be downloaded for offline use too, so the entire process can stay on your device.

There’s also a ridiculous amount of control hidden in the app’s settings. You can adjust PDF quality and compression, change how sensitive automatic document detection is, tweak auto-capture behavior, create custom file-name templates, lock the app behind biometrics, and even choose where scans are stored. It also supports bulk scanning and lets you merge, reorder, and edit pages before exporting them.

That last part is what really made Adobe feel a little excessive for what I actually need a scanner for. Adobe has plenty of advantages if you’re heavily invested in Acrobat or need its cloud and AI features, but I mostly just want to point my phone at a piece of paper and end up with a clean PDF. OSS Document Scanner does exactly that without requiring me to turn such a basic task into another subscription or cloud service.

Bitwarden

My passwords don’t need another monthly bill

Password managers are one of those apps I’m more than happy to pay for if I need to, but Bitwarden makes a pretty convincing argument that I shouldn’t have to. Its free plan lets you store unlimited passwords and use them across unlimited devices, while also giving you autofill, a password generator, passkey management, encrypted exports, and the ability to share vault items with one other person without paying anything.

That alone makes it a surprisingly capable alternative to something like 1Password or LastPass, but the fact that Bitwarden is open source is what really sets it apart for me. Its client and server code is publicly available for anyone to inspect, and if you don’t want to rely on Bitwarden’s own cloud infrastructure, you can even self-host the server yourself and keep your vault infrastructure under your own control. Your vault is protected using end-to-end, zero-knowledge encryption, so Bitwarden itself shouldn’t be able to see what you’ve stored inside it.

The Android app covers pretty much everything I actually want from a password manager too. It can save and autofill passwords in apps and websites, store cards, identities, and secure notes, generate credentials, and even save and autofill passkeys on supported versions of Android.

Open source doesn’t necessarily mean completely free, though, and Bitwarden does have a Premium tier. Features like the integrated TOTP authenticator, encrypted file attachments, emergency access, and more detailed vault-health reports require a subscription. Even so, the actual password-management part of the app is remarkably unrestricted on the free plan, and that’s ultimately the part I’d otherwise be paying another service for.

Organic Maps

Getting from A to B doesn’t require Google

Google Maps is one of those apps I’d always assumed would be nearly impossible to replace, but Organic Maps gets surprisingly close. It’s a completely free and open-source navigation app built on OpenStreetMap data, with detailed maps you can download and use entirely offline. There are no ads, trackers, mandatory accounts, or data collection either.

The fact that it works offline doesn’t mean you’re limited to simply looking at a map. Organic Maps supports turn-by-turn navigation with voice guidance for driving, walking, and cycling, along with public transport routes, offline search, hiking trails, cycling paths, contour lines, and elevation profiles. You can also import and export bookmarks and tracks using formats like GPX, KML, KMZ, and GeoJSON.

Organic Maps obviously can’t completely replicate everything Google Maps does. If I’m looking for live traffic information, detailed business reviews, or trying to figure out which restaurant nearby is actually worth going to, I’m

probably still opening Google Maps. But for simply getting somewhere, particularly somewhere I might not have reliable internet access, Organic Maps has made me realize just how much of Google Maps I don’t actually need.

LocalSend

The file-sharing app ecosystems should’ve given us

I like LocalSend enough that I’ve already written an entire article about it, and I still can’t recommend it enough. It’s essentially the cross-platform file-sharing tool I’ve always wanted AirDrop and Quick Share to be. Instead of locking you into one ecosystem, LocalSend works across Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, and Linux, so I can send a file from practically any device I own to any other one.

Using it is almost suspiciously simple. As long as both devices are connected to the same local network and have LocalSend open, they automatically discover each other. You choose a file, tap the device you want to send it to, accept the transfer on the other end, and you’re done. In my own testing, I actually found the whole process more seamless and at times faster than AirDrop, particularly because I wasn’t waiting around for the device I wanted to send something to finally appear.

The part I appreciate most, though, is that there’s no cloud involved. LocalSend discovers devices over your local network and transfers files directly between them rather than uploading them to some external server first. Its protocol uses HTTPS for encrypted transfers, and you don’t need an account or even an internet connection for it to work.

That also means I no longer need to send files to myself through Slack, WhatsApp, Google Drive, or some other service just because the two devices in front of me happen to run different operating systems. LocalSend does one incredibly simple thing, does it exceptionally well, and doesn’t care whose logo is on the devices I’m using.

The above are just a few of the open-source apps I absolutely can’t get enough of, and they’ve made it surprisingly easy to ditch some of the mainstream alternatives I’d been using for years.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most of the repetitive work in my day takes only a few minutes. For example, creating meeting minutes and turning them into tasks isn’t a major job. Neither is cleaning up the Downloads folder nor switching off the lamps, fans, and TV before going to bed. At any one time, the total is small enough that it barely registers.

The time starts to look very different when these tasks repeat after every meeting, every download, and at the beginning or end of each day. Several small jobs clubbed together become a surprisingly time-consuming exercise, even though each one looks harmless on its own. I started adding tiny automations to remove them from my routine. Some save a few minutes, and others save only a few seconds, but over time, they’ve given me back almost an entire weekend.

Turning meetings into tasks

Because action items shouldn’t die in a transcript

Writing meeting minutes is only half the job. After a call, I still need to find every action item, assign it to the right person, add a deadline, and copy it into whatever task manager I’m using. Doing this after one meeting doesn’t take much time, but several meetings can leave a decent amount of admin work behind.

I use Notion AI Meeting Notes to record and transcribe my meetings. Once a meeting ends, it generates a summary and identifies the action items discussed during the call. Since I already manage my work in Notion, I can use an automation to turn those action items into entries in my task database. Each task can include the meeting name, owner, deadline, and a link to the original notes.

You can build a similar workflow with Otter or Fireflies if you don’t use Notion for recording. The extracted tasks can stay inside the meeting tool or move to Notion, Google Tasks, or another supported task manager.

Whisper transcribed a two-hour meeting on my laptop in four minutes, and none of it left the room

And the transcription was quite good.

2
By  Anurag Singh

Making the Downloads folder organize itself

Let the files decide where they belong

The Downloads folder is easily the biggest mess on my PC. Everything I download lands there, including PDFs, images, installers, documents, ZIP files, and random attachments with names that tell me absolutely nothing.

Automating this requires a consistent file-naming convention and a folder structure that makes sense. For example, a name such as 2026-09-20_client_invoice.pdf tells me what the file contains and when I downloaded it. My folders can then separate work files by client or project, and add receipts, installers, images, and personal documents into their own locations.

You can use a folder automation tool like Sortly or a small script for this task. It can rename files using their date, source, file type, or existing metadata, and then move them into the appropriate folder.

Setting up renewal and expiry reminders

Future me shouldn’t pay for forgotten dates

Renewal and expiry dates are perfect candidates for automation because they’re predictable. Things like subscriptions, free trials, warranties, and domains all come with a date that can be recorded as soon as I receive it. However, remembering that date after a few months is where things usually fall apart.

I keep these dates in a Notion database. Each entry includes the service or document name, its renewal or expiry date, the amount I’ll be charged, and a link to the relevant website. I use an automation to then create reminders at fixed intervals, such as 30 days and seven days before the date. Something like a free trial needs a shorter reminder, while a passport or driving license needs a longer notice.

The same workflow can start from an email. For example, you can create an automation that automatically creates a reminder for emails containing terms such as “renewal date,” “expires on,” or “free trial."

Text expansion to cut out repetitive typing

A few keystrokes beat typing it all again

I type the same pieces of text far more often than I notice. My email address is the obvious example, but the same applies to my phone number, address, website, calendar link, and other details I regularly enter into forms or messages.

Text expansion lets me assign a short trigger to each piece of text. For example, typing ;email can insert my full email address, while ;address can expand into my complete mailing address. I use a prefix such as a semicolon to prevent ordinary words from triggering the expansions.

The same setup also works for longer text. I can create snippets for repeated email replies, introductions, meeting details, directions, invoice notes, or any other paragraph I regularly reuse. Text replacement is already available in the keyboard settings on many phones and computers, and you can use dedicated apps to sync a larger collection of snippets across devices.

Making the shopping list appears when I reach the store

The list appears exactly when I need it

Shopping reminders are far more useful when they appear near the shop instead of at an arbitrary time. If I remember that I need batteries while I’m working, a reminder at 6 p.m. doesn’t help because I may not be anywhere near a store. I’ll probably dismiss it and forget about the batteries again.

I keep separate lists for places such as the supermarket, pharmacy, and hardware store. Each list is linked to the relevant location, so my phone displays it when I enter the surrounding area. Anything I add during the week stays there until I’m actually in a place where I can buy it.

On my iPhone, I use the built-in Reminders app for this. I keep a reminder called “Check this list” inside each shopping list, tap Location, search for the relevant store, choose Arriving, and adjust the perimeter on the map. Reminders then displays the notification whenever I enter that area, and opening it takes me directly to the list.

Using smart plugs to handle bedtime and morning routine

Even dumb appliances can follow a schedule

I have several appliances that need to be switched off before I go to bed and turned back on in the morning. This includes lamps, fans, the TV, and my sound system. It doesn't take long to do this, but walking around and switching everything off every night is cumbersome, especially when I’m already in bed and remember that I left something running.

A smart plug can automate this even when the appliance itself isn’t smart. I connect the relevant devices to compatible smart plugs, group them inside the companion app, and create a schedule for the entire group. In my case, everything switches off around midnight and turns back on at 7 a.m. The plugs can still be controlled manually from the app if I need to override the schedule.

This works particularly well with appliances that resume their previous state once power returns. The plug also needs to support the power draw of whatever is connected to it. I keep heaters, cooking equipment, and other appliances that shouldn’t run unattended out of this routine.

Automate the things you keep repeating

I now look for automation whenever I catch myself repeating the same steps. If a task has a clear trigger and always ends the same way, spending a few minutes setting up a rule is usually worth it.

The time saved by one automation is easy to dismiss. However, the payoff becomes obvious after several of them have been running for weeks or months, quietly removing the same admin work every time it returns. I would rather spend an afternoon setting these up once than keep giving the same chores a few minutes every day.

item.title: Disabling Claude Code's memories is the best upgrade I ever made to my AI coding setup
item.itunes:title: Disabling Claude Code's memories is the best upgrade I ever made to my AI coding setup
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Claude Code can inspect a codebase, make changes across several files, and test its own work without needing every step spelled out. That level of autonomy is what makes it such a useful coding tool. Auto memory sounds like a natural addition to all of this. Claude could save useful details from one session and carry them into the next, which means I wouldn’t have to repeat the same preferences, corrections, and project context every time.

However, auto memory hasn't really been very convenient for me. In fact, I've been watching it derail my projects in real time. It gives Claude another collection of assumptions to consult, including ones that were outdated, overly specific, or no longer relevant to the work in front of it. I eventually disabled the feature, and that ended up being the best upgrade I’ve made to my AI coding setup.

Claude Code was remembering the wrong things

And that made things worse

Claude Code’s Auto Memory is separate from the instructions stored in CLAUDE.md. The feature watches for details it considers useful, such as corrections, working preferences, project decisions, and references that might matter later. It then writes those details to a memory directory associated with the repository. Claude loads the first part of its MEMORY.md index at the start of every conversation, and it can retrieve more detailed notes as it works.

The problem is that Claude decides what qualifies as a useful memory, which means even a temporary instruction can easily become a lasting preference. I could tell Claude to avoid a particular approach while debugging one issue, then start another session and find it still working around a restriction that no longer applied.

Claude would sometimes remember a discussion as a decision. I often use it to explore several ways of implementing something before choosing one, and those conversations include plenty of ideas that never make it into the project. Auto memory then preserves one of those ideas without the surrounding uncertainty. Several sessions later, Claude would treat it as part of the project’s architecture even though I had never approved or implemented it.

I wouldn’t say Auto memory caused an obvious failure on its own. However, it sent me into a loop where I had to redo a task and re-prompt Claude Code to do something the way I wanted because it had decided to follow what it had logged in memory. That, in turn, increased my usage, so over a longer playoff event, this becomes a problem.

Claude Code's real power comes from the tweaks nobody wants to talk about

Claude Code gets better when you stop chasing flashy workflows and start tightening the boring setup details.

5
By  Jeff Butts

CLAUDE.md is all the memory I need

You can add all the relevant context to this file

I still want Claude Code to understand how a project works when I start a new session. I keep the important context in CLAUDE.md so I can see exactly what Claude is told before it touches the code. Claude Code now also supports AGENTS.md, which makes it easier to carry the same project instructions across different coding agents.

My CLAUDE.md contains information that should remain true across the project, such as the package manager I use, the commands required to test changes, and any architectural rules that aren’t immediately clear from the repository. If something changes, I update the file instead of waiting for Claude to notice that one of its memories is outdated.

Writing these instructions myself also forces me to decide whether a correction deserves to become a permanent rule. If Claude repeats the same mistake, I can add a short and specific instruction to prevent it. It's also important not to clutter CLAUDE.md, because too much information can become a problem of its own. A lot of people keep adding unnecessary details when the file is really meant for key instructions Claude needs to follow consistently. It's generally recommended to keep each file under 200 lines, since shorter instructions generally lead to better adherence.

I want every session to start clean

That somehow makes Claude Code work better

Auto memory assumes that the next Claude Code session is a continuation of the previous one. That isn’t how I always use it. Carrying the reasoning and restrictions from older tasks doesn’t always give Claude a useful head start. It gives the new task baggage.

A clean session is also easier to debug. If Claude makes a strange decision, I can check my prompt, inspect the repository, and review the project instructions. Those are visible sources of context that I can correct. item.itunes:title: I stopped relying entirely on my NAS temperature warnings
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The home lab builds I've been reading about lately share an unlikely hero. It isn't a fancy drive or a shiny rack. It's a small thermometer that costs less than $30. It sits on a shelf next to some of the best hard drives for network storage. Owners calibrate these cheap sensors with real care, and some even add live temperature readouts to their server dashboards.

I don't own a rack, so I read what the drive makers published. It turned out they all agreed a thermometer should be on the rack. Though for an entirely different reason.

I disabled NAS drive sleep mode after watching the load-unload cycles destroy a $200 drive

Letting my NAS drives sleep reduced the power consumption, but it also decreased their lifespan.

3
By  Jasmine Mannan

Cooler hard drives don't really last longer

Google counted more than 100,000 of them to check

Think of a hard drive as the milk in your fridge. The FDA says a fridge should sit at or below 40°F. Nobody frets over whether theirs runs at 36°F or 38°F, because the milk doesn't care. It only cares when the fridge stops working.

Hard drives turn out to be a lot like that milk. In 2007, Google published a study of more than 100,000 drives in its data centers. It logged each drive's own temperature reading for nine months. Warmer drives did not fail more often. In fact, cooler drives failed slightly more. Only the hottest drives flipped that pattern, and mostly once they were three or more years old.

Backblaze ran the same check in 2014 on more than 34,000 drives. Across all of them, it found no link between temperature and failure. One older Seagate model was the exception. Its takeaway was simple: inside the allowed range, running cooler doesn't buy you much.

I'll be honest, I expected the opposite. Keeping drives cool is the first thing every build guide preaches. But if a few degrees don't matter, then the thermometer on that shelf needs a better reason to exist.

A cheap thermometer beats the drive's own reading

One tells you what happened, the other tells you why

Watching only your drive temperature is like waiting for milk to go bad before you notice the fridge broke. The drive tells you it is hot, but not why.

It is better to monitor the room and catch problems like a turned-off air conditioner or an open door, early. That is exactly why a thermometer should sit on your shelf.

Just be careful where you put this room thermometer. As it checks the whole space, it can miss hot spots.

So put it right where the server pulls in cool air, and not on top of the case. That way, it checks the air your drives actually breathe.

The drive makers list more dangers than heat

Cold and damp, both made the spec sheet

Here comes a surprise after I went through spec sheets of many hard drives. Seagate’s IronWolf Pro manual, for its biggest NAS drives, sets a ceiling of 140°F (60°C). That's the number most people remember.

The next line is the one I'd missed. It limits how fast the temperature can change: no more than 36°F (20°C) in an hour. A slow summer drift is fine; an open fridge door is not. The same manual sets a floor of 50°F (10°C), too, and asks for humidity between 5% and 95% with no condensation.

Seagate's limits refer to the drive-reported temperature. The air in the room will always sit a little cooler than that.

Remember Google's odd finding that cooler drives failed more? The makers clearly weren't surprised. Cold and damp both get their own lines.

Western Digital’s WD Red Plus data sheet adds the cost of heat. It rates the drives from 32°F to 149°F (0°C to 65°C). But its reliability estimate assumes a drive running at 104°F (40°C), and the fine print says that estimate drops above it.

A cheap room sensor logs exactly these things: temperature, how fast it moves, and humidity. That covers most of the spec sheet, for under $30.

NAS already watches drive temperatures, so why bother?

Because its alarm goes off after the milk is warm

You bother because the NAS warning fires late, at the drive, after the room has already gone wrong. Still, this is the best argument against the cheap thermometer, and it deserves a fair hearing. Most NAS software already reads drive temperatures and can warn you.

Synology's own help page says its boxes show high heat in orange, and may shut down to avoid damage if it continues. That's a real safety net, and it costs nothing. If your server lives in a cool, air-conditioned room, it's probably enough.

But go back to the fridge. Synology's warning is the milk starting to smell. By the time a drive reports high heat, it has been climbing for a while. Recall that 36°F-per-hour line from the Seagate manual in the gallery above. A room sensor can flag the climb early, while there's still time.

Again, if the data has been overwhelming, below is a summary table.

Between the two, you're covered from the room to the drive. The milk stays cold because someone is watching the door.
